title: The Carmelites of Compiègne (1794)
hookLine: sixteen nuns go to the guillotine singing during the French Revolution

cards: Singing rises over the noise of a Paris crowd. Carts roll toward the guillotine in this season of the Revolution. The crowd is used to shouting, to jeering, to fear.
But the women in these carts are singing Latin hymns, the way they sang them in their chapel. Tradition says the crowd grew quiet. These are Carmelite nuns from the town of Compiègne, north of Paris.
Their convent was closed. Their habits were taken. They are going to their deaths, and they are singing.

teach.b: First, the closed convent. The revolutionary government shut down religious houses, and the Carmelites of Compiègne were turned out.
They split into small groups in town, wore ordinary clothes, and kept praying their hours together as best they could.
Second, the offering. Before the danger came close, their prioress, Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine, proposed that the community offer themselves to God for peace, for France and for the Church.
Tradition says some sisters were afraid at first. In the end, they joined. Third, the trial.
They were arrested, taken to Paris and brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal.
Among the charges was fanaticism. Tradition says one sister asked what the word meant, was told it meant attachment to their religion, and was glad to be condemned for that.

Fourth, the scaffold. Tradition says they sang the Veni Creator on the way, and at the foot of the scaffold each sister knelt before the prioress, renewed her vows, and climbed, while those still waiting sang on.

teach.h: O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.
teach.b: One of the songs tradition gives them is a short psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people." The Church later declared them blessed, and Pope Francis declared them saints.

Their story was retold in a play by Georges Bernanos and an opera by Francis Poulenc, Dialogues of the Carmelites. But before any stage, there was a real cart, real voices, and a hymn that didn't stop.

how: Carmelite communities and other Catholics remember the martyrs of Compiègne on their feast day, and performances of Poulenc's Dialogues of the Carmelites keep their story before audiences far beyond the Church.

games.q: the Carmelites of Compiègne — tap the pairs.
p: the play and opera that retold it

s: the Carmelites of Compiègne are only characters in an opera
they were real nuns, put to death in the Revolution. the opera came later.
tradition says the prioress went last
each sister renewed her vows before her, then climbed.
the nuns went to their deaths in silence
tradition says they sang, and the crowd grew quiet.

games.q: you're a Carmelite of Compiègne. your convent has been closed and your habit taken. what do you do?
o: go home to your family and stop praying the hours.
stay with your sisters in town and keep praying together, quietly.
games.why: they stayed in small groups in Compiègne, in ordinary clothes, and kept praying together, until their arrest.

practice: Bring to mind something hard in front of you, a conversation, a test, a diagnosis, a long day, and hum or sing very quietly one line of a song or hymn you know by heart: not a performance, just a voice held steady.
Notice what happens to your breathing as you sing. If you pray, sing the psalm's line the Carmelites sang; if not, any steady song will do.

wordCard.voice: Laudate Dominum. Praise the Lord, the opening of the psalm tradition says the Carmelites of Compiègne sang on their way to the guillotine.

orig.note: Latin: praise the Lord, the opening of the short psalm tradition says they sang.

carryVoice: Your line: singing to the scaffold. They sang on the cart the hymns they had sung in their chapel. Day eight hundred seventy-three, done.
